  int<lower=1> S; // number of subgroups
  int<lower=1> K; // number of observations in each subgroup
  matrix<lower=0,upper=1>[S,K] O[G];

  real sigmaS;
  real c;
  real d;

> but must be greater than 0
>

>

Stan requires all transformed parameters to satisfy
their declared constraints at the end of the transformed
parameter statements.

Your transformed parameter a is declared to be positive.
But its definition will produce a negative result whenever

sigmaS > mu - mu*mu.

If you need to keep parameter a positive, then declare sigmaS to
satisfy the necessary constraint with

real<lower=0, upper=(mu - mu * mu)> sigmaS;

Stan's constraint language is limited by the fact that the
constraints have to be declared in order. But that'll work
here.

Better yet, find an alternative simpler way to parameterize
the model.

- Bob

parts:
On Friday, February 22, 2013 4:43:33 PM UTC-5, rubi wrote:
I followed your advice and set the constraint on sigmaS and deleted the sampling from beta(1,1). I also changed sigmaS to be sampled from beta instead of from gamma, because sigmaS is the variance of beta distributed observations. (See code below)

Since sigmaS is now bounded from above by mu * (1 - mu) < 1, a beta distribution for sigmaS is problematic because it puts positive mass in the region from mu * (1 - mu) to 1. Since the amount of mass is not a constant but a function of the unknown mu, this mismatch affects the log-posterior and the partial derivatives thereof. This may be related to the error you are getting.

Thus, at a minimum, you should truncate your beta prior to the [0,mu * (1 - mu)] interval, which may entail a noticeable slowdown because the beta CDF is somewhat expensive to evaluate. Alternatively, you could just omit the explicit prior on sigmaS if an implicit uniform prior between 0 and mu * (1 - mu) is acceptable to you.

Ben

p(c) propto pow(Exponential(c|1), G)

What is c?

That error arises when the sampler can't move at all
from 100 different tries at random initialization.

It can sometimes come from values being too extreme
which can cause arithmetic issues.

You need to scope each of your variables properly
in loops.

for (g in 1:G){
c ~ exponential(1);
d ~ exponential(1);
for (s in 1:S){

//mu ~ beta(1,1);
//sigmaS ~ beta(c,d);
lp__ <- lp__ - log1m(1-pow((1-pow(mu - mu * mu,c)),d));

for (k in 1:K){
O[g,s,k] ~ beta(a,b);
}
}
}

All of the sampling statements other than the one
for O[g,s,k] should be outside the loop.

I don't understand why you're making the priors for
a and b so complicated. A more natural way to do this
with an exponential scale would be:

parameters {
real<lower=0> lambda;
real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;

real<lower=0> a;
real<lower=0> b;
}

model {
lambda ~ exponential(1); // use any prior with support on (0,inf)
theta ~ beta(1,1); // can remove because it's uniform and theta bounded
for (g in 1:G)
for (s in 1:S)
for (k in 1:K)

O[g,s,k] ~ beta(lambda*theta,lambda*(1 - theta));
}

The standard deviation isn't particularly natural for
beta because it's bounded. The variable theta will
get the hierarchical mean and lamda the hierarchical
prior count. Andrew suggested a Pareto prior on lambda
in Bayesian Data Analysis (chapter 5, which starts with
a very similar model), but I don't think he likes that choice
any more.

You can make it faster by vectorizing the last loop, but
I wouldn't worry about that until you have a version
working.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: One of therror messages "stan::math::poisson_log: Rate parameter is -73.6109, but must be >= 0!"
parts: This is because constraints can't be declared in the model block. You'd have to do it in parameters or transformed parameters.
